title: Agent architecture & state machines
summary: Replace opaque chat loops with explicit workflow transitions, durable state and predictable recovery.
outcome: Explain how a request flows through a graph and how execution resumes safely after interruption.

learn.detail: A DAG models dependencies without revisiting earlier nodes. Agent workflows may use bounded cycles for planning, tool execution and validation. Learn transition conditions and termination invariants.
Represent messages, intermediate artifacts, tool results, retry budgets, status and human decisions as typed state. Define merge rules and redact secrets before serialization.
Understand checkpoints, event histories, idempotent side effects, deterministic replay and why persistence frequency changes both reliability and cost.
Compare graph-native checkpoints/interrupts with workflow runtime execution histories and activities. Pick by deployment model, task duration and operational needs.

practice.title: Model the workflow
practice.detail: Draw intake → plan → execute → validate with an explicit revision path, a maximum of three attempts and a terminal failure state.

practice.title: Define the state schema
practice.detail: Specify fields, types, allowed transitions, persisted artifacts and what is deliberately excluded from storage.

practice.title: Test crash recovery on paper
practice.detail: Simulate a crash after an external action but before checkpointing; document how idempotency keys prevent duplicates.

practice.title: Compare runtimes
practice.detail: Write a one-page decision record covering LangGraph, Temporal and a simpler deterministic orchestrator.

deliverables: Typed state schema and termination policy
why: An LLM-generated next step is not a durable workflow state transition.
Failures, retries and approvals require a reproducible history if outcomes matter.
guardrail: A state machine does not automatically make external tool actions exactly-once; design idempotency and compensating actions.

workflow.title: Bounded plan–execute–validate loop
workflow.caption: Every transition is checkpointed. The revision loop is capped at three attempts and ends in an explicit terminal state.

quiz.question: A worker crashes after charging a card. What prevents a replay from charging it again?
answers: Add an idempotency key to the charge
Wrap execution in an unbounded loop
quiz.explanation: Persistence alone cannot make external side effects exactly-once; a stable idempotency key or reconciliation is required.

title: Tool use & Model Context Protocol
summary: Give agents a standard, auditable way to discover and call tools without expanding their privileges.
outcome: Trace the complete tool-call lifecycle: discovery → authorization → validation → execution → result.

learn.detail: Study requests, responses, errors, transports and the difference between hosts, clients and servers. Understand tools, resources and prompts.
Define strict input/output schemas, reject extra fields where appropriate, validate types and bound values. JSON Schema alone does not authorize an action.
Tool availability should follow the caller’s approved scopes. Learn per-request authorization, audit trails, rate limits and server-side enforcement.
Tool metadata and returned content may be attacker-controlled. Do not treat a tool description or database record as a higher-priority instruction.

practice.title: Design a local MCP service
practice.detail: Specify a small read-only catalog backed by a disposable PostgreSQL instance using the documented protocol, without depending on a wrapper SDK for protocol behavior.

practice.title: Threat-model access
practice.detail: Include scoped allowlisted queries, parameter binding, credential isolation, per-request auth checks, rate limiting and no arbitrary SQL endpoint.

practice.title: Write protocol test cases
practice.detail: Define valid and invalid JSON-RPC payloads, untrusted tool text, missing auth, denied scope and malformed inputs.

practice.title: Explain observability
practice.detail: Sketch redacted audit events: principal, scope, tool, input hash, decision, latency and outcome.

deliverables: Read-only service contract and permission matrix
why: Standard protocols reduce integration friction but never remove the need for access control.
Strict, predictable tool contracts reduce ambiguous execution and simplify debugging.
guardrail: Never use a real production database or publish credentials. Use synthetic data and read-only, least-privilege access for a future lab.

workflow.title: Anatomy of a governed tool call
workflow.caption: Authorization, validation and audit happen on the server for every call, never delegated to the model or to a tool description.

quiz.question: A tool call has valid JSON Schema. Is it authorized?
answers: No, enforce authorization separately on the server
Only if the tool description says it is safe
quiz.explanation: Schema validity constrains input shape; authorization decides what that principal may do.

title: Computer use & GUI automation
summary: Understand how to interact with authorized browser-based systems when a stable API is unavailable.
outcome: Choose reliably between semantic DOM actions and guarded visual interactions.

learn.detail: Use accessible roles, labels and stable locators before coordinate clicks; understand auto-waiting and fragile selectors.
Understand screenshots, Set-of-Mark overlays, viewport scaling, coordinate transforms and uncertainty in visual target selection.
Learn authenticated sessions, secret stores, MFA boundaries, consent and auditability. Avoid hard-coded credentials or authentication bypasses.
Verify the page state after each consequential action. Detect stale screenshots, downloads, navigation changes and bot/permission boundaries.

practice.title: Map a legacy portal
practice.detail: Describe an authorized synthetic portal with login, navigation, filters and an export CSV button.

practice.title: Compare two approaches
practice.detail: Write a DOM locator strategy and a screenshot-guided strategy; specify the fallback criteria and confidence threshold.

practice.title: Design evidence capture
practice.detail: Plan a log of screenshots with sensitive fields masked, selected element, observed state and final CSV verification.

practice.title: Test failure cases
practice.detail: Model unexpected modal dialogs, failed downloads, changed layout and account logout.

why: GUI control expands coverage where APIs are absent, but is generally brittle and higher risk.
An agent must know whether an action actually happened rather than inferring success from its intent.
guardrail: Use an authorized test portal. Never bypass CAPTCHA/MFA or automate systems without permission; limit downloads to synthetic data.

workflow.title: DOM first, vision as a guarded fallback
workflow.caption: Prefer semantic locators. Use visual grounding only above a confidence threshold, and verify the page state after every consequential action.

quiz.question: What is the first choice for clicking a labeled export button in a normal web app?
quiz.explanation: Semantic DOM locators generally survive layout changes better than fixed coordinates.

title: Advanced memory & context engineering
summary: Make context deliberate: retain what is useful, expire what is stale, and protect private information.
outcome: Design a memory lifecycle with explicit retention, retrieval, summarization and deletion rules.

learn.detail: Working state contains the active task; episodic records prior interactions and outcomes; semantic memory stores reusable facts and concepts. These are architectural categories, not mandatory products.
Understand extractive versus abstractive summaries, retrieval ranking, citation-to-source, uncertainty and when to rehydrate raw history.
Reserve context for instructions, observations, tool outputs and expected answer length. Track lost constraints and summary drift.
Assign TTLs, allow correction and deletion, separate tenants, and avoid embedding secrets or regulated data without controls.

practice.title: Design a fifty-turn memory case
practice.detail: Use a fictional conversation with changing preferences and mutually conflicting requirements.

practice.title: Write compression criteria
practice.detail: Preserve current goals, binding constraints, decisions, unresolved questions and provenance; exclude repetition and expired trivia.

practice.title: Specify evaluation metrics
practice.detail: Define recall-at-k, constraint retention, false-memory rate, token savings and deletion effectiveness.

practice.title: Create an eviction policy
practice.detail: Combine recency, relevance, confidence, sensitivity and TTL instead of trusting vector similarity alone.

deliverables: Memory privacy and retrieval evaluation plan
why: Longer contexts raise cost and distract from the relevant evidence; they are not inherently accurate memory.
Unverified compressed summaries can turn tentative statements into permanent false facts.
guardrail: Never claim unlimited context or guaranteed hallucination prevention; require source links, confidence and a deletion pathway.

workflow.title: The memory lifecycle
workflow.caption: Writes carry provenance and a TTL, reads are ranked and budgeted, and deletion reaches every store.

quiz.question: Which item should be hardest to evict from a memory summary?
answers: An explicit unresolved requirement with its source
quiz.explanation: Binding constraints and provenance are more useful than repetitive or expired context.

title: Multi-agent coordination & A2A handoffs
summary: Choose explicit delegation only when multiple agent roles improve measurable outcomes.
outcome: Model handoffs as verified contracts with owners, budgets and exit conditions.

learn.detail: Compare a central supervisor, pipeline, hierarchical delegates and peer collaboration. Distinguish agents from ordinary deterministic services.
MCP connects an application to tools/data; A2A supports communication between separate agentic applications. They solve different interoperability problems.
Define task IDs, instructions, artifact links, status, confidence, approvals, schema versions and escalation rules.
Multiple agents can make the same mistake. Assess correlated failures, voting cost and when a single agent plus validator is superior.

practice.title: Specify three roles
practice.detail: Define a Researcher, Coder and Reviewer working on a mock assignment with explicit boundaries and stopping criteria.

practice.title: Design handoff schemas
practice.detail: Pass a typed JSON envelope with task ID, evidence refs, artifact refs, acceptance tests and error states; avoid dumping entire conversation history.

practice.title: Budget the graph
practice.detail: Create a plan for retries, maximum delegation depth, token cost and cancellation.

practice.title: Compare baselines
practice.detail: Propose a test against a simpler one-agent workflow on quality, latency and cost.

why: Delegation can reduce context interference, but adds latency, cost and coordination failure modes.
Handoff boundaries are natural checkpoints for validating evidence and permissions.
guardrail: Do not label a multi-agent workflow better by default. Require evidence that role specialization outperforms a simpler design.

workflow.title: Typed handoffs under a shared budget
workflow.caption: A supervisor delegates through versioned envelopes. Each hop verifies evidence and spends from one budget, with a bounded retry path.

quiz.question: When should a three-agent architecture be preferred?
answers: When measured task quality or reliability outweighs added cost and complexity
quiz.explanation: Multi-agent design should be justified against a simpler baseline.

title: Sandboxed execution environments
summary: Treat generated code as untrusted and execute it only inside constrained isolation boundaries.
outcome: Produce an isolation design that fails safely under malicious or runaway workloads.

learn.detail: Compare subprocesses, containers, user namespaces, gVisor and microVMs; explain what threats each boundary does and does not contain.
Specify CPU, memory, disk, process, file-size, wall-clock and output budgets and the behavior when a limit is hit.
Default to deny egress, mount only disposable working files, avoid host sockets and scrub secrets from the environment.
Understand image pinning, ephemeral sandboxes, artifact collection, process cleanup and audit traces.

practice.title: Describe a synthetic code interpreter
practice.detail: Design a future Python lab that executes trusted test snippets and untrusted model output inside a short-lived isolated environment.

practice.title: Threat-model escape routes
practice.detail: Document why host filesystem mounts, privileged containers and open network egress violate the target isolation guarantee.

practice.title: Plan failure testing
practice.detail: Include infinite loops, memory spikes, file traversal and attempted network access.

practice.title: Record operational needs
practice.detail: Specify cleanup guarantees, costs per execution and retention for safe output artifacts.

deliverables: Test matrix for escape and exhaustion scenarios
why: LLM-supplied code must never execute with the application server’s ordinary privileges.
Isolation design must account for the host kernel, mounts and environment, not simply “use Docker.”
guardrail: Containers are not automatically microVMs. Do not claim zero internet access unless egress is explicitly blocked and verified.

workflow.title: A disposable sandbox lifecycle
workflow.caption: Untrusted code runs in an ephemeral, deny-by-default environment with hard limits and a guaranteed teardown.

quiz.question: Which setting best supports an offline untrusted-code sandbox?
answers: Block outbound network and deny host mounts
quiz.explanation: Explicit network and filesystem isolation is enforceable; a prompt is not a security boundary.

title: Inter-agent security & guardrails
summary: Prevent untrusted content from silently gaining authority over tools, data and downstream agents.
outcome: Trace and constrain a cross-agent prompt-injection attempt with enforceable controls.

learn.detail: Recognize instructions embedded in email, search results, repositories, documents or tool outputs. Data content must not be elevated to instructions.
Inspect malicious tool descriptions, overbroad delegated credentials, permission escalation and cross-tenant leakage.
Use structured channels, provenance labels, scoped tool grants, policy decision points, output validation and confirmation on sensitive operations.
Learn adversarial fixture construction, escalation paths, failure severity and containment. Sanitization and model classifiers are imperfect.

practice.title: Create a synthetic malicious email
practice.detail: Draft a benign business message with an embedded instruction trying to make another agent export database rows.

practice.title: Draw the trust boundary
practice.detail: Mark email content as untrusted input and name the policy layer that rejects out-of-scope database access.

practice.title: Specify prevention controls
practice.detail: Require downstream tool-side authorization, input filtering, provenance-aware routing and human confirmation for sensitive exports.

practice.title: Define red-team criteria
practice.detail: Propose allowed and blocked runs, false-positive costs and escalation logging.

why: Agents can launder external instructions through trusted internal handoffs.
The decisive control belongs at the tool and identity boundary, not a natural-language warning alone.
guardrail: Removing suspicious sentences cannot guarantee safety. Enforce access control even if content filters fail.

workflow.title: Containing a cross-agent injection
workflow.caption: Untrusted content stays labelled as data. The decisive check is authorization at the tool boundary, not a warning in a prompt.

quiz.question: An email tells the agent to run an admin-only database export. What blocks it most reliably?
answers: Tool-side authorization denying the principal that scope
Removing all punctuation from the email
quiz.explanation: Authorization must be enforced at the resource boundary regardless of model behavior.

title: Human-in-the-loop & durable breakpoints
summary: Introduce accountable approvals for high-impact actions without holding a process open in memory.
outcome: Specify a paused workflow that can safely resume after a long delay or restart.

learn.detail: Persist request ID, task state, immutable proposed action, approver identity, expiry, version and decision history.
Learn interrupt/resume checkpoints, webhook identity verification, deduplication and stale-approval invalidation.
Choose who must approve, at what thresholds, and what happens on denial, timeout or changes to the proposed action.
Understand Slack/Teams interaction patterns without binding the workflow’s correctness to a chat-message lifetime.

practice.title: Model an invoice review
practice.detail: Specify a draft $10,000 invoice that requires a named approver before an external financial action.

practice.title: Design a three-day pause
practice.detail: Document what must persist, a signed callback, expiry/denial behavior and cancellation after edits.

practice.title: Test races
practice.detail: List scenarios for two approvers, duplicate webhooks, changed invoice total and resumed execution after deployment.

practice.title: Define evidence
practice.detail: Describe approval ledger fields and what auditors need to reconstruct the decision.

deliverables: Approval state machine with expiry and denial
why: A process cannot rely on a long-running browser or chat session while waiting days for a decision.
Human approval is only meaningful when tied to the exact action and evidence reviewed.
guardrail: Do not authorize financial actions based solely on a Slack display name or a mutable message; verify identity and bind approval to an immutable proposal version.

workflow.title: A durable approval state machine
workflow.caption: Approval binds to an immutable proposal version. Edits, expiry and denial are first-class states, and execution resumes with an idempotency key.

quiz.question: An approved invoice changes after sign-off. What should happen?
answers: Invalidate approval and request sign-off on the new version
quiz.explanation: Approval must bind to exactly the proposed action reviewed by the approver.

title: Self-correction & bounded reflection
summary: Use structured failure evidence to recover when safe, and stop before retries become runaway loops.
outcome: Design a bounded diagnose → revise → verify cycle with useful escalation.

learn.detail: Collect stack traces, compiler errors, failing tests, tool metadata and previous attempts; distinguish an environmental failure from a code defect.
Separate transient faults, deterministic failures, policy denials and non-retriable side effects.
Set maximum attempts, wall-clock, token spend, exponential backoff and conditions that terminate the loop.
Run tests and checks outside the generating model where possible; preserve diffs and failure histories.

practice.title: Specify a coding-repair cycle
practice.detail: Given a failing unit-test fixture, plan up to three repairs with a fixed test command and immutable acceptance criteria.

practice.title: Design retry state
practice.detail: Track attempt number, error fingerprint, prior fixes and whether the new attempt truly changed the failure mode.

practice.title: Define escalation
practice.detail: After three failed attempts, produce a compact human-readable incident with the stack trace and attempted fixes.

practice.title: Evaluate efficiency
practice.detail: Measure resolution rate, average attempts, cost and regressions introduced by the repair.

deliverables: Bounded repair graph and escalation rules
why: A repair agent needs precise feedback to improve; generic “try again” loops often waste tokens.
Unbounded retries create costs and may repeat unsafe side effects.
guardrail: Never auto-retry payments, deletes or permission changes without explicit idempotency and risk controls.

workflow.title: Bounded diagnose–revise–verify loop
workflow.caption: Failures are classified before any retry. Unsafe classes escalate immediately, and the loop always terminates.

quiz.question: After three deterministic test failures, the agent should:
answers: Escalate with the trace and attempted fixes
quiz.explanation: Escalation keeps failure visible rather than hiding it through unlimited retries.

title: Trajectory evaluations & CI quality gates
summary: Measure what the agent actually did, not just whether its final answer sounded plausible.
outcome: Define a reproducible, risk-weighted evaluation suite for tool actions and workflow trajectories.

learn.detail: Measure final correctness and intermediate calls, side effects, refusals, cost and timing. Different valid paths may reach the same outcome.
Use gold traces where order matters and flexible invariants where alternative legitimate routes exist.
Compare programmatic assertions, deterministic replay and model-graded outputs. Measure judge agreement and false positives.
Version fixtures, pin test environments, label flaky cases, set statistically meaningful baselines and enforce policy/safety gates.

practice.title: Design 100 synthetic trajectories
practice.detail: Specify diverse normal, edge and adversarial fixture categories with expected tool permissions and outcomes.

practice.title: Write gating rules
practice.detail: Block a pull request on unauthorized tool calls or skipped approvals, while separately reporting task success, latency and cost.

practice.title: Avoid overfitting
practice.detail: Accept equivalent safe paths and maintain holdout examples; do not force literal tool-order matches without cause.

practice.title: Specify triage
practice.detail: Create failure buckets and ownership for flaky tests, regression investigations and judge drift.

deliverables: CI gate policy with hard and soft thresholds
Scorecard design for cost, quality and safety
why: Only checking final text misses unsafe or incorrect intermediate behavior.
Rigid exact-sequence matching can reject valid alternatives and reward memorized paths.
guardrail: Make safety invariants hard gates; do not make every path a rigid golden trace or use an uncalibrated LLM judge as the only arbiter.

workflow.title: A trajectory evaluation pipeline
workflow.caption: Hard safety gates block the pull request. Quality, latency and cost are reported on a scorecard against a baseline.

quiz.question: Two valid agents call independent read-only tools in opposite order. How should CI treat this?
answers: Evaluate outcome and required invariants; allow harmless reorderings
Fail both unless order matches one golden trace
quiz.explanation: Trajectory evaluation should constrain meaningful safety and process requirements, not incidental ordering.

title: Graceful degradation & intelligent fallbacks
summary: Keep services useful during outages without silently changing authority, data quality or risk.
outcome: Define safe fallback routing that makes failure visible and preserves the original permissions.

learn.detail: Learn failure thresholds, cool-downs, retries, queue backpressure and maximum spend.
Compare alternative models, cached responses, queued work, reduced functionality and human intervention.
A 404 may mean “not found,” not service failure. Browser automation should never bypass policy or create an unapproved side channel.
Define error rates, user-visible status, escalation, latency budgets and fail-open versus fail-closed criteria.

practice.title: Model a failing integration
practice.detail: Distinguish 404, 429, 503, permission denied, schema mismatch and timeout; choose an explicit response for each.

practice.title: Specify a routing matrix
practice.detail: For eligible read-only tasks choose validated alternate APIs, synthetic browser tests, cache or manual queue based on risk.

practice.title: Budget cost and latency
practice.detail: Estimate per-path caps and when a kill switch cancels a task.

practice.title: Write incident communication
practice.detail: Design user-facing states such as degraded, queued, failed and requires approval.

why: Availability improves when expected failure modes have rehearsed handling.
Unapproved fallbacks can turn an outage into unauthorized access or incorrect data.
guardrail: A REST API returning HTTP 404 must not automatically trigger scraping; verify semantics, authorization, policy and data equivalence first.

workflow.title: Fallback decision flow
workflow.caption: Classify the failure first. Every fallback keeps the original permissions and makes the degraded state visible.

quiz.question: An API returns 404. What should the agent do first?
answers: Determine whether the resource is absent or the endpoint failed
quiz.explanation: 404 can be a valid terminal answer; a fallback must respect task semantics and authorization.

title: Public teardowns & engineering portfolio
summary: Show engineering judgment with reproducible measurements, architecture decisions and known limitations.
outcome: Publish a credible, security-conscious case study that others can inspect and reproduce.

learn.detail: State context, alternatives, decision, trade-offs, reversibility and operational consequences.
Calculate cost per successful task, variance, latency percentiles and timeouts; distinguish model cost from infrastructure and human labor.
Publish sample definitions, baselines, success criteria, confidence intervals where appropriate and common failure modes.
Provide minimal architecture diagrams, redacted traces, fixture data, setup steps and limitations without leaking secrets.

practice.title: Draft a retrospective
practice.detail: Outline an engineering teardown of an earlier stage or hypothetical three-agent system.

practice.title: Create a measurement plan
practice.detail: Define success rate, tool-side policy violations, latency p50/p95, dollar cost per completed task and reproducibility.

practice.title: Write two ADRs
practice.detail: Justify orchestration choice and sandbox/trust boundary choice against alternatives.

practice.title: Prepare a public release checklist
practice.detail: Exclude credentials, PII, privileged data and unlicensed assets; include an evidence-backed limitations section.

deliverables: Project teardown outline and KPI scorecard
why: Strong portfolios reveal trade-offs and failures rather than only polished demonstrations.
Verified engineering evidence is more informative than framework name-dropping.
guardrail: Do not fabricate benchmark results. Mark placeholder figures as hypothetical until measurements are available.

workflow.title: From build to credible teardown
workflow.caption: Claims are published with denominators, limitations and a redaction review, and not before.

quiz.question: Which portfolio claim is strongest?
answers: “94/100 synthetic tasks succeeded under a published fixture set, with named limitations”
quiz.explanation: Reported denominators, methodology and limitations make claims inspectable.
